items.label: f01-no-scheduler
items.front: Who drains Harbor's webhook outbox and wakes snoozed conversations, and how much does one dispatch call do?
items.back: Nobody automatically: there are only manual endpoints (wake-due, dispatch); the hosted services handle publication and exports. DispatchAsync claims one ready delivery at a time under a lease, at most 50 per call, serially, with limited retries - so eventual delivery is not promised.

items.label: f04-two-writer-conflict
items.front: Walk two writers through Harbor's optimistic concurrency: both load V1, A saves first. What happens to B, and what does the API return?
items.back: A's save changes the version; B's update still uses V1 as the original token, matches no row, and EF throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException, which the API maps to 409.

items.label: f02-evidence-statement
items.front: What is the testing workshop's evidence-statement template?
items.back: Given [fixture], when [operation], assert [observable result]. This catches [defect]. It does not prove [limit].

items.label: f03-fixture-row-purpose
items.front: In the queue filter test, why add an unrelated conversation that contains no search term?
items.back: Without it, a broken 'return everything' implementation could pass. Each fixture row should have a clearly different job: name the incorrect implementation it catches.

items.prompt: A test asserts that the list endpoint and the overview endpoint agree for several filters. Why is that not enough?

choices.text: Parity tests are flaky, because the two endpoints read in different transactions
List paging means the two endpoints can never agree on totals in the first place
If both forget the workspace predicate they agree while leaking another tenant's data
The overview rounds its counts, so exact parity with the list can never be asserted

choices: Parity tests are flaky, because the two endpoints read in different transactions
List paging means the two endpoints can never agree on totals in the first place
If both forget the workspace predicate they agree while leaking another tenant's data
The overview rounds its counts, so exact parity with the list can never be asserted

items.explanation: Parity proves consistency, not correctness. Check totals too: aggregates can leak without returning the foreign row.

items.prompt: Harbor appends Id ascending to every supported conversation ordering. What does that fix, and what does it not?

choices.text: It makes ordering total so static data pages reproducibly; a changing queue can still repeat or skip rows
It freezes the queue, so later pages can never repeat or skip a row even while writers insert
It turns offset paging into keyset paging, because Id is now the cursor
It only speeds the query up by letting SQLite walk the primary key index

choices: It makes ordering total so static data pages reproducibly; a changing queue can still repeat or skip rows
It freezes the queue, so later pages can never repeat or skip a row even while writers insert
It turns offset paging into keyset paging, because Id is now the cursor
It only speeds the query up by letting SQLite walk the primary key index

items.explanation: Rows can tie on timestamps; a unique order is required for pagination. Inserts or removals before the current offset still shift pages - a cursor or snapshot addresses that.

items.prompt: Why do the List and Overview endpoints build their result set from one shared conversation query component?

choices.text: So EF can cache one compiled query plan shared by both endpoints
So both endpoints interpret the same filter identically
Because Infrastructure projects may never reference controller code
So the overview can reuse the list's paging and tag loading

choices: So EF can cache one compiled query plan shared by both endpoints
So both endpoints interpret the same filter identically
Because Infrastructure projects may never reference controller code
So the overview can reuse the list's paging and tag loading

items.explanation: The controller chooses how to use the query (List adds ordering, tags, paging; Overview adds an aggregate); the shared component defines which conversations belong.

items.prompt: The overview returns open, snoozed, closed, unassigned and total for one filtered population. Which relation holds?

choices.text: open + snoozed + closed + unassigned = total, since each conversation is in one bucket
Each count ignores its own filter, the way search facets do
total counts only the conversations on the current list page
open + snoozed + closed = total; unassigned overlaps them

choices: open + snoozed + closed + unassigned = total, since each conversation is in one bucket
Each count ignores its own filter, the way search facets do
total counts only the conversations on the current list page
open + snoozed + closed = total; unassigned overlaps them

items.explanation: The overview is not a set of facets; with state=Open the closed count is simply zero.

items.prompt: You must test 'at the SLA deadline' versus 'one tick later'. What approach does the workshop recommend?

choices.text: Move the machine clock forward from inside the test host process
Run the test repeatedly and accept it if most of the runs pass
Sleep 100 ms past the deadline, then assert that the breach was recorded
Pass exact now values around the deadline into the domain methods

choices: Move the machine clock forward from inside the test host process
Run the test repeatedly and accept it if most of the runs pass
Sleep 100 ms past the deadline, then assert that the breach was recorded
Pass exact now values around the deadline into the domain methods

items.explanation: Domain methods take now. A real-clock sleep cannot reliably establish a one-tick boundary.

items.prompt: A valid API key for workspace A is sent to a list route for workspace B. Why can the scope filter answer 403 without querying whether B exists?

choices.text: It first loads workspace B and returns 403 only when B exists, otherwise 404
It compares the route's workspace with the caller's workspace claim, without touching the database
It returns 404 for every workspace mismatch, so that existence is never revealed to callers
The authentication handler already rejected the key with 401 before the filter could run

choices: It first loads workspace B and returns 403 only when B exists, otherwise 404
It compares the route's workspace with the caller's workspace claim, without touching the database
It returns 404 for every workspace mismatch, so that existence is never revealed to callers
The authentication handler already rejected the key with 401 before the filter could run

items.explanation: WorkspaceScopeFilter's 403 is a claim comparison. By-ID endpoints are different: they fold ID and caller workspace into one lookup and answer 404 (ADR 0002).

items.prompt: page and size each bind successfully as int, but their product can overflow. How does Harbor compute the paging offset safely?

choices.text: It uses checked int arithmetic and lets the OverflowException become a 500
It multiplies in int, then casts the product to long before Skip
It widens page to long before subtracting and multiplying
It multiplies in int and rejects the request when the result is negative

choices: It uses checked int arithmetic and lets the OverflowException become a 500
It multiplies in int, then casts the product to long before Skip
It widens page to long before subtracting and multiplying
It multiplies in int and rejects the request when the result is negative

items.explanation: The cast must happen before the multiplication; casting the product only widens a value that may already have overflowed. Harbor also returns an empty page when the offset is beyond the count.

items.prompt: A queue has 500 matching conversations and the page size is 2. If the implementation applied the filter AFTER paging, what would you expect?

choices.text: Two rows and X-Total-Count 500, just slower
The same rows but in a different order
Too few rows on the page and a wrong X-Total-Count
A 400 because the page size is smaller than the match count

choices: Two rows and X-Total-Count 500, just slower
The same rows but in a different order
Too few rows on the page and a wrong X-Total-Count
A 400 because the page size is smaller than the match count

items.explanation: Membership, order and page are different operations. Filtering after paging can return too few rows and the wrong total; counting after paging only counts that page.

items.prompt: The list endpoint counts the matches, then fetches one page. What does that two-statement design imply?

choices.text: The page is fetched first so the count can skip the rows already returned to the client
The total is computed in memory from the rows on the fetched page
The count and the page always agree, because EF runs both statements in one implicit transaction
A writer between the two statements can change the data, so it is not an export snapshot

choices: The page is fetched first so the count can skip the rows already returned to the client
The total is computed in memory from the rows on the fetched page
The count and the page always agree, because EF runs both statements in one implicit transaction
A writer between the two statements can change the data, so it is not an export snapshot

items.explanation: They are separate statements; nothing freezes the data between them. A snapshot is a different requirement (see the export jobs).

items.prompt: A webhook receiver wants to ignore deliveries it has already processed. What should it deduplicate on?

choices.text: The signing timestamp, since each delivery attempt is signed exactly once
The HMAC signature, which is unique for every delivery Harbor sends
Nothing: reject anything older than the timestamp tolerance instead
A stable delivery identifier, because the signing timestamp can change per attempt

choices: The signing timestamp, since each delivery attempt is signed exactly once
The HMAC signature, which is unique for every delivery Harbor sends
Nothing: reject anything older than the timestamp tolerance instead
A stable delivery identifier, because the signing timestamp can change per attempt

items.explanation: HMAC proves integrity and a timestamp tolerance limits old replays; neither establishes that the delivery was never processed before.

items.prompt: Harbor queues webhook deliveries in the same database save as the conversation change. What does that guarantee?

choices.text: The subscriber receives each webhook exactly once, even across dispatcher crashes and retries
The HTTP call to the subscriber is rolled back as well whenever SaveChangesAsync fails
Deliveries are sent inline over HTTP, before SaveChangesAsync returns to the controller
The change and its queued delivery commit together, but the subscriber is not in the transaction

choices: The subscriber receives each webhook exactly once, even across dispatcher crashes and retries
The HTTP call to the subscriber is rolled back as well whenever SaveChangesAsync fails
Deliveries are sent inline over HTTP, before SaveChangesAsync returns to the controller
The change and its queued delivery commit together, but the subscriber is not in the transaction

items.explanation: This is a transactional outbox: Webhooks.cs adds pending delivery entities and does not send HTTP inline.

items.prompt: HarborApiFactory builds the test schema with EnsureCreated. What can the HTTP suite therefore miss?

choices.text: A model change with no migration: tests pass on today's model while existing databases never change
Foreign-key violations, because EnsureCreated disables constraint checking in SQLite
Any SQLite translation problem, because EnsureCreated switches the suite to an in-memory provider
Seed data problems, because EnsureCreated deletes all rows after each test class

choices: A model change with no migration: tests pass on today's model while existing databases never change
Foreign-key violations, because EnsureCreated disables constraint checking in SQLite
Any SQLite translation problem, because EnsureCreated switches the suite to an in-memory provider
Seed data problems, because EnsureCreated deletes all rows after each test class

items.explanation: Development startup uses migrations; that is why the separate MigrationDriftTests guard exists. A clean migration test still differs from upgrading a populated database.

items.prompt: A refactor moves ToListAsync() before the Where/OrderBy/Take calls, and the endpoint still returns the same rows. What changed?

choices.text: A bounded query became a full-table load, with filtering and paging done in memory
Nothing; EF defers ToListAsync until the last LINQ operator has been applied
The query now fails at runtime, because Take cannot be called after ToListAsync
Only the SQL formatting changed; the database still applies the WHERE and the limit

choices: A bounded query became a full-table load, with filtering and paging done in memory
Nothing; EF defers ToListAsync until the last LINQ operator has been applied
The query now fails at runtime, because Take cannot be called after ToListAsync
Only the SQL formatting changed; the database still applies the WHERE and the limit

items.explanation: IQueryable describes database work; ToListAsync executes it. Materialising early can preserve the visible result while changing the cost completely.

items.prompt: A conversation-list request carries a well-formed segment GUID that does not exist in the caller's tenant. Which response does it get, and at which stage?

choices.text: 422 ProblemDetails from the controller, once BuildAsync returns null
404 from the workspace scope filter, since the segment is not visible
400 from model binding, before the controller action ever runs
403, because the segment belongs to another tenant than the API key

choices: 422 ProblemDetails from the controller, once BuildAsync returns null
404 from the workspace scope filter, since the segment is not visible
400 from model binding, before the controller action ever runs
403, because the segment belongs to another tenant than the API key

items.explanation: Malformed values (bad dates, unknown sort names, reversed bounds) fail binding/validation with 400 before the action. A missing segment has a valid shape, so it reaches the controller, which keeps the 422 contract.

items.prompt: How should the createdFrom / createdBefore bounds be interpreted, and why?

choices.text: createdFrom <= CreatedAt < createdBefore, so adjacent windows neither overlap nor leave a gap
createdFrom < CreatedAt < createdBefore, excluding both edges to avoid duplicates
Both bounds compare last-activity time, truncated to the day
createdFrom <= CreatedAt <= createdBefore, with the end set to 23:59:59.999

choices: createdFrom <= CreatedAt < createdBefore, so adjacent windows neither overlap nor leave a gap
createdFrom < CreatedAt < createdBefore, excluding both edges to avoid duplicates
Both bounds compare last-activity time, truncated to the day
createdFrom <= CreatedAt <= createdBefore, with the end set to 23:59:59.999

items.explanation: A half-open window composes cleanly. An invented .999 end-of-day can miss rows because the database can store more precision; bounds describe creation time, not last activity.

items.prompt: Conversation has a version token and conflicting tracked writes raise a 409. A human reads a page, a colleague edits it, then the first human submits an update. What happens?

choices.text: It fails with 409, because the browser sent the version it originally read
It normally succeeds and overwrites, because the new request loads the latest version
The second request blocks until the colleague's transaction has closed
EF merges both edits field by field, keeping each human's changes

choices: It fails with 409, because the browser sent the version it originally read
It normally succeeds and overwrites, because the new request loads the latest version
The second request blocks until the colleague's transaction has closed
EF merges both edits field by field, keeping each human's changes

items.explanation: The token protects overlapping tracked database writes inside the server. No edit token travels to the browser, so conditional writes would be needed.
